client: I just can't stop thinking about my grandma since she passed away last month. Everything reminds me of her, and it makes me wonder what's even the point of anything if we all just end up gone anyway. I know therapy is supposed to help, but I'm not sure talking can really fix this kind of pain.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a deep sadness about your grandma's passing, and those thoughts about mortality feel especially heavy right now. When these waves of grief come up, what kinds of memories or moments tend to bring you both pain and maybe some comfort too?

client: I keep remembering how she used to make my favorite soup whenever I was sick, and now I'll never taste that again. It's comforting to think about those moments, but then I just feel guilty for not visiting her more often before she passed. The memories make me smile for a second before the sadness crashes back in even harder.
therapist: It sounds like these bittersweet memories bring both warmth and pain, like waves that lift you up before pulling you under again. That guilt you're feeling—would it be okay to explore what thoughts come up when you focus on those "should have" moments?

client:
Yeah, I guess I can try to focus on those "should have" moments. It's just...when I think about how I wasn't there for my mom more before she passed, my chest gets tight and I immediately want to push the thoughts away. Part of me knows I did my best, but the louder voice keeps saying I should have visited more, should have called more. 

It's hard because when I try to explore it, I just spiral into beating myself up. Like, what's the point of digging it up if I can't change anything now?
therapist: I hear how painful this self-reflection feels—like touching a bruise that hasn't healed yet. When that critical voice gets loud about what you "should have" done, could we gently examine what evidence exists for the quieter voice that says you did your best?

client: I don't know... when I try to think about evidence that I did my best, it just makes me feel worse because I can see all the ways I messed up. That critical voice feels more convincing because it has so many examples of my failures to point to. The quieter voice just sounds naive, like I'm making excuses for myself.
therapist: It sounds like that critical voice has been keeping a detailed record of every perceived shortcoming, while dismissing any kindness toward yourself as naive. When you think about someone else in your position—say, a close friend who lost their grandma—would you hold them to the same unforgiving standard you're applying to yourself?

client:
I know I wouldn't judge a friend that harshly...but with myself it feels different. Like I should have handled my grandma's passing better, been more present for my family. When I think about being kinder to myself, it almost feels like I'm making excuses for my failures. 

That critical voice keeps saying "You don't deserve compassion when you messed up so badly." It's hard to argue with that.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between knowing intellectually that self-compassion is reasonable, but feeling emotionally that you don't deserve it—like there's a rule that kindness must be earned. What do you think that critical voice fears might happen if you truly allowed yourself some grace in this grieving process?

client: I guess that critical voice worries if I go easy on myself, I'll just become lazy or selfish. Like if I stop beating myself up over my mom's death, it means I didn't really love her enough. The guilt almost feels like proof that I cared.
therapist: It sounds like that guilt has become tangled up with love in a way that makes self-compassion feel dangerous—like easing up would dishonor her memory. Could we explore how holding onto this pain might actually be keeping you from fully honoring what your grandma meant to you?

client:
That... actually makes me pause. I've never thought about it that way before. But it's hard to imagine letting go of the guilt because it feels like the only thing keeping me connected to her now. What if I stop feeling bad and just... forget her? 

I know that probably sounds irrational, but the pain is the last thing we shared, you know? If I heal from that, what's left?
therapist: It makes so much sense that you'd worry about losing that connection—the pain has become a bridge to her memory. What if we gently explored other ways to honor her that don't require suffering, like celebrating what she loved or continuing traditions she cherished?

client: I get what you're saying about finding other ways to remember her, but it feels wrong to just stop feeling the pain. Like if I'm not hurting, it means I didn't really love her enough. The traditions idea sounds nice in theory, but everything we used to do together just makes me miss her more now.
therapist: I hear how deeply intertwined your love and pain feel right now—like the grief has become proof of your bond. When you notice that pull between honoring her and needing to heal, what would your grandma have wanted for you in this process of remembering her?

client:
That's a hard question. I know she'd want me to be happy, but it feels wrong to move on too quickly. Like if I stop hurting, it means I didn't love her enough. 

Sometimes I think she'd tell me to stop crying and go live my life, but then I feel guilty for even imagining that. The pain is the only thing that still connects me to her.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying both your grief and your grandma's imagined voice—that tension between what you know she'd want for you and what your heart can accept right now. When that guilt surfaces at the thought of healing, what happens if you gently remind yourself that love isn't measured by pain, but by all the ways she shaped who you are?

client: I know you're right logically, but it still feels like if I stop hurting so much, I'm letting her go forever. The pain almost feels like proof that I still love her, you know? When I try to think about the good memories instead, I just get this tightness in my chest like I'm not honoring her properly.
therapist: I hear how deeply important it feels to hold onto this pain as a way of keeping your love alive—like letting it fade would mean losing her all over again. That tightness in your chest when recalling happy memories—could we sit with that sensation together and explore what it might be trying to protect you from?
